MCP-PostgreSQL-Ops

 Give Claude and other AI assistants read-only PostgreSQL observability for
 slow queries, locks, bloat, VACUUM, indexes, replication, WAL, and capacity.

 

 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 

---

 What is MCP-PostgreSQL-Ops?

MCP-PostgreSQL-Ops lets Claude, OpenWebUI, and other MCP clients inspect a
PostgreSQL server through natural-language questions. It turns requests such as
“Which tables need VACUUM now?” into predefined, read-only SQL queries and
returns the evidence needed to diagnose the database.

- Read-only tools: no arbitrary SQL execution or data-changing operations.
- PostgreSQL 12–18: version-specific views and columns are detected
 automatically.
- Useful without extensions: core monitoring works immediately;
 pg stat statements and pg stat monitor add query analytics.
- Deployment choice: install a Claude Desktop extension, run with uvx , or
 connect OpenWebUI directly to the HTTP MCP server.

For an AI-generated code walkthrough, use
 .

 What can you ask?

 

 More requests to try: see Example Queries for requests
by area (performance, health checks, capacity and VACUUM, structure,
troubleshooting, multi-step workflows) and per-tool examples.

Core tools work with normal catalog access. Broader cross-database visibility
depends on the PostgreSQL role; use a least-privilege monitoring account in
production.

 Example: slow-query evidence and recommendations 

 

More examples are available in the
screenshots and usage wiki.

is the shortest. Option B provides a complete local demonstration with sample
databases and OpenWebUI.

 

 Option A: Claude Desktop extension (fastest)

Requirements: Claude Desktop with extension support and a PostgreSQL server
reachable from the computer running Claude Desktop.

1. Open the latest
 GitHub Release
 and download mcp-postgresql-ops- .mcpb .
2. In Claude Desktop, open Settings → Extensions → Advanced settings →
 Install Extension… and select the downloaded file.
3. Enter the PostgreSQL host, port, user, password, and default database.
4. Ask Claude: Show the current active PostgreSQL connections. 

The password field is marked sensitive and is stored by Claude Desktop. The
extension runs the server locally over stdio ; it does not expose an HTTP
port.

install.title: Quick Start
install.html:
Choose one path. If you already have PostgreSQL and Claude Desktop, Option A is the shortest. Option B provides a complete local demonstration with sample databases and OpenWebUI.

Option A: Claude Desktop extension (fastest)

Requirements: Claude Desktop with extension support and a PostgreSQL server reachable from the computer running Claude Desktop.

  1. Open the latest GitHub Release and download mcp-postgresql-ops-<version>.mcpb.
  2. In Claude Desktop, open Settings → Extensions → Advanced settings → Install Extension… and select the downloaded file.
  3. Enter the PostgreSQL host, port, user, password, and default database.
  4. Ask Claude: Show the current active PostgreSQL connections.

The password field is marked sensitive and is stored by Claude Desktop. The extension runs the server locally over stdio; it does not expose an HTTP port.

Option B: OpenWebUI 0.13 with the included demo database

Requirements: Git, Docker with the Compose plugin, and an OpenWebUI model provider whose model supports tool calling.

1. Configure

git clone https://github.com/call518/MCP-PostgreSQL-Ops.git
cd MCP-PostgreSQL-Ops
cp .env.example .env
cp mcp-config.json.http mcp-config.json.http.local
chmod 600 mcp-config.json.http.local
openssl rand -hex 32   # use the output as WEBUI_SECRET_KEY
vi .env                # set WEBUI_SECRET_KEY; adjust ports if needed

mcp-config.json.http.local is ignored by Git and is mounted only into MCPO. If REMOTE_AUTH_ENABLE=true, replace <REMOTE_SECRET_KEY> in that local file with the same secret configured in .env. Leave the tracked mcp-config.json.http file as a credential-free template.

The default .env.example credentials are only for the included disposable PostgreSQL demo. Do not reuse them for an existing or externally reachable database.

2. Start

docker compose up -d
docker compose ps --all  # wait for mcp-server to be healthy and init to exit 0

This starts OpenWebUI at http://localhost:3003, the MCP server at http://localhost:18003/mcp, optional MCPO/OpenAPI compatibility at http://localhost:8003, and a disposable PostgreSQL demo environment. The demo includes ecommerce, analytics, inventory, and HR data plus intentional bloat and index patterns for realistic monitoring questions.

3. Connect OpenWebUI to the MCP server

  1. Open http://localhost:3003, create the administrator account, and add a model provider under Settings → Admin → Connections:

    • OpenAI: add an OpenAI API connection with URL https://api.openai.com/v1, enter your OpenAI API key (Auth Bearer), set API Type to Chat Completions, and save it.
    • Ollama on the Docker host: the Compose file already points OpenWebUI to http://host.docker.internal:11434; ensure Ollama is reachable from Docker and pull a tool-capable model.

    Confirm that the model appears in a new chat before continuing.

  2. The Quick Start calls tools through Chat Completions with model reasoning turned off, using this default already present in .env.example:

    DEFAULT_MODEL_PARAMS={"reasoning_effort":"none"}

    This value requires API Type: Chat Completions. With Responses, OpenWebUI 0.13.0 still sends reasoning_effort, and every request fails with Unsupported parameter: 'reasoning_effort'. If the open-webui-data volume already exists, set the same value under Settings → Admin → Models → Model Defaults → Model Parameters because its saved database value takes precedence. To keep model reasoning through Responses instead, see OpenAI reasoning models.

  3. Under Settings → Admin → Tools → Integrations → External Tool Servers, add a connection of type MCP (Streamable HTTP) with URL http://mcp-server:8000/mcp and authentication None. This matches the Quick Start default REMOTE_AUTH_ENABLE=false; enable and configure Bearer authentication before exposing the server outside the local Docker host.

  4. Under Settings → Admin → System → Interface → Chat, enable Tool Search and Defer Built-in Tools, then set Deferral Threshold to 0. This keeps the full PostgreSQL tool list within the model's tool limits.

  5. In a new chat, enable the connection under Integrations → Tools and ask: Use mcp-postgresql-ops to show tables that need VACUUM.

If setup or tool calls fail, see OpenWebUI Issues for existing-volume precedence, per-model and per-chat overrides, and provider compatibility notes.

MCPO is optional. OpenWebUI 0.13 connects to the MCP server directly and does not require the MCPO proxy. To expose the tools as an OpenAPI/Swagger service for a legacy client, use MCPO at http://localhost:8003. The Compose file starts it so every project keeps the same deployment layout. To run without it, use docker compose up -d mcp-server open-webui.

To connect the Docker stack to an existing PostgreSQL server instead, update the POSTGRES_* values in .env and run:

docker compose -f docker-compose.custom-db.yml up -d

usage.title: Example Queries
usage.html:
Requests are grouped first by task area, then by tool. Each tool runs read-only queries; results depend on the PostgreSQL version, installed extensions, and the connected role's privileges.

🧭 Requests by Area

📈 Database Performance Analysis

  • "Show database-wide performance statistics"
  • "Analyze transaction commit ratios and I/O patterns"
  • "Check buffer cache hit ratios for all databases"
  • "Monitor temporary file usage and deadlock counts"

🔧 Background Writer & Checkpoints

  • "Analyze checkpoint performance and timing"
  • "Show background writer efficiency statistics"
  • "Check buffer allocation and writing patterns"
  • "Monitor checkpoint scheduling vs requested ratios"

🔍 Server Health Check

  • "Check PostgreSQL server status."
  • "What database am I connected to?"
  • "Show current database connection details."
  • "Verify if extensions are installed."
  • "Show current active connection count."
  • "Display PostgreSQL version and configuration."

📊 Performance Analysis

  • "Show top 20 slowest queries."
  • "Find unused indexes."
  • "Analyze recent query activity."
  • "Identify performance bottlenecks."
  • "Show cache hit ratios for queries."

💾 Capacity Management

  • "Check database sizes."
  • "Find largest tables."
  • "Show tables that need VACUUM."
  • "Analyze disk usage by database."
  • "Display table and index sizes."
  • "Analyze table bloat and dead tuples."
  • "Show database-wide bloat summary."
  • "Check autovacuum status and trigger conditions."
  • "Monitor recent autovacuum activity patterns."
  • "Show currently running VACUUM operations."
  • "Analyze VACUUM effectiveness and maintenance patterns."

🗄️ Structure Analysis

  • "List all databases with owners."
  • "Show tables in public schema."
  • "Display user accounts and permissions."
  • "Explore database structure."

📈 Advanced Monitoring

  • "Monitor active sessions and queries."
  • "Analyze index usage efficiency."
  • "Check VACUUM and ANALYZE history."
  • "Review PostgreSQL configuration settings."
  • "Find memory-related configuration parameters."
  • "Show all logging configuration options."
  • "Search for connection-related settings."
  • "Identify connection patterns."
🩺 Troubleshooting Requests

Connection Issues

  • "Check PostgreSQL server connectivity."
  • "Verify connection parameters."
  • "Test database access permissions."

Extension Problems

  • "Check if pg_stat_statements is installed."
  • "Verify pg_stat_monitor availability."
  • "Show installed extensions status."

Performance Issues

  • "Analyze slow query performance."
  • "Check database load and connections."
  • "Review index usage efficiency."
  • "Monitor recent query patterns."
🔁 Multi-Step Workflows

Send these requests in order to run a routine review.

Regular Health Checks

  1. "Check server status and active connections."
  2. "Show top 10 slowest queries from last hour."
  3. "Verify all databases are accessible."
  4. "Check if any tables need maintenance."

Capacity Planning

  1. "Analyze database sizes and growth trends."
  2. "Identify largest tables and indexes."
  3. "Review disk usage by schema."
  4. "Plan storage capacity requirements."

Performance Optimization

  1. "Find queries consuming most resources."
  2. "Identify unused or inefficient indexes."
  3. "Analyze cache hit ratios."
  4. "Monitor query execution patterns."
🟢 Extension-Independent Tools (Always Available)

features.title: What can you ask?
features.html:
Show the current active connections and blocked sessions
Which queries consume the most execution time?
Find bloated tables and explain what needs attention first
Which tables need VACUUM or autovacuum tuning?
Show unused or inefficient indexes
Check replication, WAL, checkpoints, and background processes
Summarize database size, growth, and I/O activity
Draw the relationships for the ecommerce schema

More requests to try: see Example Queries for requests by area (performance, health checks, capacity and VACUUM, structure, troubleshooting, multi-step workflows) and per-tool examples.

Core tools work with normal catalog access. Broader cross-database visibility depends on the PostgreSQL role; use a least-privilege monitoring account in production.
